stem: Different persons can have different developmental goals because:
options: What may be development for one may not be development for another; it may even be destructive for another
Development is decided by the government only
solution: Different persons can have different developmental goals; what may be development for one may not be development for another — it may even be destructive for another. For example, a dam may bring irrigation for farmers but displace tribal families.

stem: The developmental goals that people have are not only about better income but also about other important things in life such as:
options: Equal treatment, freedom, security and respect of others
solution: People seek things like equal treatment, freedom, security and respect of others; they resent discrimination. All these are important goals — in fact, for many the quality of life is more important than money.

stem: Two people or groups of persons may seek things which are conflicting. For example, a girl expects the same freedom and opportunity as her brother, but her brother may:
options: Not like her having the same freedom
solution: Two persons may seek conflicting goals — a girl expects as much freedom as her brother and that he shares housework, but the brother may not like this. This shows different people can have different and even conflicting notions of a better life.

stem: For development, people look at a mix of goals. Besides income, which of the following would people generally want?
options: Job security, respect, freedom, equal treatment and a pollution-free environment
solution: For development people look at a mix of goals; besides seeking more income, people also seek things like security, respect of others, equal treatment, freedom, and a pollution-free environment.

stem: Money, or material things that one can buy with it, is one factor on which our life depends. But the quality of our life also depends on:
options: Non-material things such as friends, freedom, security, and a pollution-free environment
The size of one's house alone
solution: Money cannot buy all the goods and services that one needs to live well; the quality of our life also depends on non-material things such as the freedom to participate in decisions, equal treatment, and a clean environment.

stem: For comparing countries, their income is considered to be one of the most important attributes. The income of a country is the income of:
options: All the residents of the country — leading to the idea of average or per capita income
solution: For comparing countries, their income is considered one of the most important attributes; countries with higher income are more developed. Since a country has many people, we take the average income, also called the per capita income.

stem: The average income of a country, obtained by dividing the country's total income by its total population, is called the:
solution: The total income of the country divided by its total population gives the average income, which is also called the per capita income.

stem: In the World Development Report brought out by the World Bank, the criterion used for classifying countries is:
options: Per capita income or average income
solution: In the World Development Reports brought out by the World Bank, this criterion — per capita or average income — is used in classifying countries.

stem: According to the World Bank criterion used in the chapter, countries with a per capita income of a certain amount per annum and above are called:
solution: Countries with per capita income of US$ 49,300 per annum and above (as per the 2019 World Development Report) are called rich countries, while those with per capita income of US$ 2,500 or less are called low-income countries.

stem: India comes in which category of countries as per the World Bank classification used in the chapter?
solution: India comes in the category of low-middle income countries because its per capita income was only US$ 6,700 per annum in 2019.

stem: Average income is useful for comparison but it also hides disparities. Why?
options: It does not tell us how this income is distributed among people; averages can mask inequalities between the rich and poor
solution: While average income is useful for comparison, it does not tell us how this income is distributed among people; two countries with the same average income can differ greatly in how equally that income is spread. Averages hide disparities.

stem: The example of two countries with the same average income but different distributions shows that:
options: Average income is the only thing that matters
For comparing countries, average income is useful, but we also need to know how equally or unequally income is distributed
The country with more people is richer
solution: The example illustrates that if there is a big difference in the distribution of income (say one country has all citizens earning equally and another has a few very rich and many very poor), most people would prefer the more equal country — so distribution matters, not just average.

stem: The comparison of states within India — Punjab, Kerala and Bihar — shows that Kerala, despite having a lower per capita income than Punjab, has a better:
options: Human development record (lower infant mortality, higher literacy, better health)
solution: Kerala, with lower per capita income than Punjab, has a low Infant Mortality Rate, higher literacy rate and better health facilities — showing that money in your pocket cannot buy all the goods and services you need to live well, so income alone is not an adequate indicator of development.

stem: The Infant Mortality Rate (IMR) indicates the number of children that die before the age of one year as a proportion of:
solution: The Infant Mortality Rate (IMR) indicates the number of children that die before the age of one year as a proportion of 1,000 live children born in that particular year.

stem: The Literacy Rate measures the proportion of literate population in the:
solution: Literacy Rate measures the proportion of the literate population in the 7-and-above age group.

stem: The Net Attendance Ratio is the total number of children of the age group 6-10 attending school as a percentage of:
options: Total number of children in the same age group
solution: Net Attendance Ratio is the total number of children of age group 6 and 10 attending school as a percentage of the total number of children in the same age group.

stem: Money in your pocket cannot buy a pollution-free environment or ensure that you get unadulterated medicines, unless:
options: You can influence the relevant public facilities; some of the most important things are provided collectively
solution: Money cannot buy a pollution-free environment or unadulterated medicines unless you can influence what your community can provide for all — many important goods and services (public facilities) are best provided collectively rather than bought individually.

stem: The example of collective provision — such as a ration shop, or public distribution — shows the importance of:
options: Public facilities in improving people's quality of life
solution: Many of the important things in life can best be provided on a collective basis — for example, public distribution of foodgrains, collective security, or clean drinking water — showing that public facilities are essential for a good quality of life.

stem: The Human Development Report published by the UNDP compares countries based on which of the following?
options: The educational levels of the people, their health status, and per capita income
solution: The Human Development Report published by UNDP compares countries based on the educational levels of the people, their health status, and per capita income — a broader measure than income alone.

stem: UNDP stands for:
solution: UNDP stands for the United Nations Development Programme, which brings out the Human Development Report comparing countries.

stem: In the Human Development Report ranking cited in the chapter, on which measure did some poorer states/countries score better than richer ones?
options: Health and education indicators such as life expectancy and literacy
solution: The Human Development Report ranks countries on a combination of health (life expectancy at birth), education (mean and expected years of schooling), and income (per capita income) — showing that some countries/states with lower income can have better human development.

stem: Life Expectancy at birth denotes:
options: The number of years a person works
The average expected length of life of a person at the time of birth
solution: Life Expectancy at birth denotes the average expected length of life of a person at the time of birth.

stem: Per Capita Income in the Human Development Report is calculated in dollars for all countries so that it can be:
options: Compared, and is also done in a way (purchasing power parity) that accounts for differences in prices across countries
solution: For comparison between countries, incomes are calculated in dollars (using purchasing power parity), so that they can be compared, adjusting for differences in the cost of living across countries.

stem: Which state in India, though lower in per capita income than others, has one of the best records in human development indicators?
solution: Kerala has one of the best records in human development indicators (high literacy, low IMR, good health) despite not having the highest per capita income, largely because it provides adequate public facilities like health and education.

stem: The example of Kerala teaches that for the development of a region, what is important besides income?
options: Adequate provision of public facilities like basic health and educational facilities
solution: For a region's development, income is important but not enough; adequate provision of public facilities — health, education, food security — is crucial, as Kerala's example demonstrates.

stem: The Body Mass Index (BMI) is used to find out whether adults are:
solution: The Body Mass Index (BMI) is a way to find out whether adults are undernourished — one takes the weight of the person and divides it by the square of the height in metres; if this figure is less than 18.5, the person is undernourished, and if more than 25, the person is overweight.

stem: According to the BMI method, a person is considered undernourished if the figure is:
solution: If the BMI (weight divided by the square of height in metres) is less than 18.5, the person is undernourished; if it is more than 25, the person is overweight.

stem: The proportion of undernourished adults in India is quite large, which shows that:
options: Despite economic growth, a significant section of people still lack adequate nutrition
solution: A large proportion of undernourished adults in India shows that, despite economic growth, a significant section of people still lack adequate nutrition and food security — an important dimension of development that income alone does not capture.

stem: The issue of sustainability of development raises the question of whether:
options: Development can continue for the current generation only
The kind of development we are pursuing can continue without harming the prospects of future generations
solution: The question of sustainability of development is important because development must be sustained — the resources and the environment must be maintained so that future generations can also enjoy a good quality of life.

stem: The example of groundwater overuse in India shows that:
options: Overuse of a resource can lead to its depletion, threatening sustainability of development
Water is not needed for development
solution: The falling water table in many regions due to over-extraction of groundwater is an example of a resource being overused; it shows that development based on the overuse of natural resources is not sustainable.

stem: The example of crude oil (petroleum) reserves is used to illustrate that:
options: Non-renewable resources will get exhausted after a few generations, so we must think about sustainability and alternatives
solution: Crude oil is a non-renewable resource; the world's crude oil reserves will last only a few more decades at the present rate of use. This shows that consequences of environmental degradation and resource exhaustion do not respect national or state boundaries, and development must be sustainable.

stem: Renewable resources are those which:
options: Are replenished by nature, as in the case of crops and plants, up to a certain limit
solution: Renewable resources are those which get replenished or renewed by nature, e.g., crops and plants. However, even these can be overused (like groundwater) beyond the rate at which nature can replenish them, threatening sustainability.

stem: Non-renewable resources are those which:
options: Will get exhausted after years of use, since there is a fixed stock on earth which cannot be replenished
solution: Non-renewable resources are those which will get exhausted after years of use; we have a fixed stock on earth which cannot be replenished, e.g., crude oil, coal and minerals.

stem: Consequences of environmental degradation do not respect:
options: National or state boundaries — the issue is no longer region- or nation-specific
solution: The consequences of environmental degradation do not respect national or state boundaries; this issue is no longer region-specific — for example, global warming affects the entire world, making sustainability a shared global concern.

stem: Two things that became clear about development in the chapter are: (1) different people can have different developmental goals, and (2):
options: What may be development for one may not be development for another, and it may even be destructive
solution: Two things become clear: first, different people can have different developmental goals; second, what may be development for one may not be development for another — it may even be destructive for another (e.g., a factory that provides jobs but pollutes a river).

stem: The chapter argues that for comparing development, income is an important but insufficient measure; we should also consider:
options: Health, education, and other measures of quality of life and equality
solution: Income by itself is not a complete or adequate indicator of material goods and services; we should look at combined indicators like health (IMR, life expectancy), education (literacy), and how equally income and facilities are distributed.

stem: A country with a higher per capita income than another may still be considered less developed if:
options: It performs worse on health, education, environmental quality or has greater inequality
solution: A country with higher per capita income may be less developed than another if it fares worse on health, education, or environmental quality, or if its income is very unequally distributed; development is multi-dimensional, not just income.

stem: 'Sustainable development' can be described as development that:
options: Meets the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs
solution: Sustainable development means development that should take place without damaging the environment, and development in the present should not compromise with the needs of future generations.

stem: The idea that the 'earth has enough resources to meet the needs of all but not enough to satisfy the greed of even one person' is associated with which key concern of development?
options: The sustainability and equitable use of resources
solution: This Gandhian idea highlights the concern for sustainability and equity in the use of resources — resources are limited and must be used carefully so that everyone's needs are met and future generations are not deprived.

stem: In comparing different persons' notions of development, a landless rural labourer and a rich urban businessman would likely have:
options: Different goals — the labourer may want more work and fair wages, while the businessman may want cheap labour and better markets
solution: Different people have different and even conflicting developmental goals; a landless labourer values more days of work and better wages, while a businessman may value cheap labour — what is development for one may not be so for the other.

stem: The National Development of a country requires thinking about whether a programme or policy is good for:
options: The country as a whole, and whether there is a better way of doing things — considering conflicting interests
solution: National development means thinking about what is good for the country as a whole; but since different people have conflicting interests, we must consider whether a programme benefits a large number of people or just a small group, and whether there is a better alternative.

stem: The Human Development Index (HDI) combines income with which two other dimensions?
options: Health (life expectancy) and education (years of schooling)
solution: The Human Development Index (HDI) combines three dimensions: a long and healthy life (life expectancy at birth), knowledge (mean and expected years of schooling), and a decent standard of living (per capita income).

stem: Which of these best reflects why public facilities are important for development?
options: Many important things in life cannot be bought individually and are best provided collectively — like health, education, sanitation and security
solution: Public facilities like health, education, sanitation, safe drinking water and security are important for development because they cannot be adequately bought by individuals; they are best provided collectively and greatly improve people's quality of life.

stem: The chapter suggests that people prefer more income AND more of other goals. This means development is about:
options: A combination of income and other quality-of-life goals such as security, respect, freedom and a clean environment
solution: Development is about a combination of goals — people want higher income along with equal treatment, freedom, security, self-respect and a clean environment; development means improving all these aspects of life together.

stem: Why do we use averages (like per capita income) despite their limitations?
options: They are useful for comparison between countries or regions, even though they hide the distribution of income
They only apply to rich countries
solution: Averages are used for comparison because they give a single number to compare countries or regions; their limitation is that they do not reveal the distribution — how income is spread among people — so they must be used alongside other measures.

stem: A dam built for irrigation and electricity may be seen as development by some but destruction by others because it:
options: May displace people (e.g., tribal communities) and submerge forests and land, so its impact differs across groups
solution: A dam can be development for farmers who get irrigation and for cities that get electricity, but destruction for the tribal people and villagers who are displaced and lose their land, forests and livelihoods — showing conflicting notions of development.

stem: The most important point the chapter makes about measuring development is that:
options: No single indicator can capture development fully; we need to look at income, health, education, equality and sustainability together
Only the government can measure it
solution: The key point is that development is multi-dimensional — no single indicator (like per capita income) can fully capture it; we must look at a combination of income, health, education, distribution/equality, and environmental sustainability.

stem: Which of the following statements about sustainability and development is correct?
options: Environmental concerns and development are unrelated
Sustainability of development is comparatively a new area of knowledge which scientists, economists and philosophers are working together on, since resources are limited
solution: Sustainability of development is comparatively a new area of knowledge in which scientists, economists, philosophers and other social scientists are working together, because the overuse of resources and environmental degradation threaten the ability of future generations to develop.

stem: The overall conclusion of the chapter 'Development' is that development is:
options: A complex idea involving different goals for different people, best measured by multiple indicators, and must be sustainable for future generations
solution: The chapter concludes that development is a complex idea: different people have different (and sometimes conflicting) goals; income alone is inadequate, so we use combined indicators like the HDI; and development must be sustainable so that future generations are not deprived.

stem: In the World Development Report 2019, countries with a per capita income of US $12,536 per annum and above were classified by the World Bank as:
solution: According to the World Bank's World Development Report 2019, countries with per capita income of US $12,536 per annum and above are called rich or high-income countries.

stem: In the World Bank classification (2019), countries with a per capita income of US $1,035 or less were called:
solution: Countries with per capita income of US $1,035 or less per year are classified as low-income or poor countries by the World Bank criterion used in the chapter.

stem: India, with its level of per capita income, falls in which category as per the World Bank classification in the chapter?
solution: India comes in the category of low-middle income countries because its per capita income in 2019 was well below the threshold for high-income countries.

stem: The average income of a country, obtained by dividing the country's total income by its population, is called:
solution: The average income of a country is the per capita income, calculated by dividing the country's total (national) income by its total population.

stem: The main criterion used by the World Bank to classify countries in its World Development Report is:
solution: In the World Development Report, the World Bank uses per capita income (average income) as the main criterion for classifying countries as high, middle or low income.

stem: A major limitation of using average (per capita) income to compare countries is that it:
options: Hides disparities in the distribution of income among people
solution: Average income is a useful measure for comparison, but it does not tell us how income is distributed among people; it hides the disparities between the rich and the poor.

stem: The Infant Mortality Rate (IMR) indicates the number of children who die before the age of one year out of every:
solution: Infant Mortality Rate (IMR) indicates the number of children that die before the age of one year as a proportion of 1,000 live children born in that particular year.

stem: Among Punjab, Kerala and Bihar, the state with the highest per capita income (in the chapter's data) is:
solution: In the chapter's comparison of Indian states, Punjab has the highest per capita income, followed by Kerala, while Bihar has the lowest.

stem: Despite not having the highest per capita income, __________ has the best social indicators like low IMR and high literacy, according to the chapter.
solution: Kerala, though lower in per capita income than Punjab, has a very low infant mortality rate and high literacy, showing that money alone does not ensure human development.

stem: The literacy rate measures the proportion of the literate population in the:
solution: The literacy rate measures the proportion of the literate population in the 7-and-above age group of a country or region.

stem: The Human Development Report is published by the:
solution: The Human Development Report, which compares countries based on educational levels, health status and per capita income, is published by the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP).

stem: The Human Development Index (HDI) combines per capita income with which two other dimensions?
solution: The HDI combines three dimensions of development: a decent standard of living (per capita income), a long and healthy life (life expectancy), and knowledge (education/years of schooling).

stem: 'Life Expectancy at birth' denotes:
options: The average expected length of life of a person at the time of birth
The number of births per year
solution: Life Expectancy at birth denotes the average number of years a newborn is expected to live, an important indicator of the health status of a population.

stem: To measure whether adults are undernourished, the __________ is calculated by dividing weight (kg) by the square of height (metres).
solution: The Body Mass Index (BMI) is used to find out whether adults are undernourished; it is calculated by dividing a person's weight (in kg) by the square of the height (in metres).

stem: According to the BMI method, an adult is considered undernourished if the BMI is:
solution: If a person's Body Mass Index is less than 18.5, then he or she would be considered undernourished; if it is more than 25, the person is overweight.

stem: Sustainable development is best described as development that:
options: Meets present needs without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their needs
solution: Sustainable development means that development should meet the needs of the present generation without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs.

stem: The example of falling groundwater levels in many parts of India is used to show that:
options: Overuse of a renewable resource can still make it unsustainable
solution: Though groundwater is a renewable resource, its over-exploitation beyond the rate of recharge has led to falling water tables across India, illustrating that even renewable resources need sustainable use.

stem: Assertion (A): Two countries with the same average income may still differ in development. Reason (R): Average income hides how income is distributed and ignores other goals like health and education.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
solution: Two countries with equal average income can differ greatly in development because average income does not reveal income distribution or non-income goals like health, education and environment — R explains A.

stem: Assertion (A): Money cannot buy all the things needed for a good quality of life. Reason (R): Things like a pollution-free environment and security often depend on collective or public provision.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
solution: Money in your pocket cannot buy a pollution-free environment, freedom from disease, or peace; these depend on collective provision, so income alone is not enough for a good life — R explains A.

stem: Different persons can have different and even conflicting notions of development because:
options: A decision that is development for one may not be so, or may even be destructive, for another
solution: People have different developmental goals, and what may be development for one person can be destructive for another — for example, a dam may benefit some farmers but displace others.

stem: Public facilities like schools, hospitals and a public distribution system are important for development because they:
options: Provide services that individuals cannot easily buy on their own
solution: Many important things for a good life — public health, education, safety — are provided collectively; people cannot buy pollution-free air or good public services individually, so public facilities are vital.

stem: The example of Kerala versus states with higher income teaches that:
options: Higher income alone does not guarantee a better quality of life
Income is the only measure of development
Health and education do not matter
solution: Kerala, with a lower per capita income than some states, has a low IMR and high literacy, showing that better health and education facilities matter as much as income for the development of a region.

stem: The consequences of environmental degradation, such as global warming, are significant because they:
options: Do not respect national or state boundaries
solution: Environmental degradation is an issue that goes beyond states and countries; the consequences of, for example, global warming affect the whole world and do not respect national boundaries.

stem: Per capita income is used for comparing countries despite its limitations because:
options: It gives a single, comparable summary measure of average prosperity
solution: Per capita income is used because it provides a simple and comparable summary figure of a country's average income, though it must be supplemented with other indicators for a fuller picture.

stem: For development, people look at a mix of goals; besides income these include:
options: Security, respect, equal treatment, freedom and a good environment
solution: People desire not only higher income but also equal treatment, freedom, security, respect from others, good health, education and a clean environment — a mix of goals defines development.

stem: The example of a landless rural labourer and a prosperous farmer wanting different things illustrates that:
options: Developmental goals differ according to a person's situation
solution: A landless labourer may want more days of work and better wages, while a prosperous farmer may want a good support price and cheap labour — showing developmental goals depend on one's circumstances and can conflict.

stem: The Human Development Report ranks countries on the basis of the Human Development Index; a higher rank indicates:
solution: In the Human Development Index ranking, countries are ordered so that a higher rank (nearer to 1) reflects better performance in income, health and education combined — that is, higher human development.

stem: The idea attributed to Mahatma Gandhi, that 'the earth has enough to satisfy everyone's needs but not everyone's greed', supports the principle of:
solution: Gandhi's idea highlights that resources are sufficient for everyone's needs but not for endless greed, underscoring the need for sustainable and equitable use of resources.

stem: The proportion of undernourished adults in India, according to the chapter, is:
options: Quite large, indicating a big challenge for development
solution: The chapter notes that the level of undernourishment among adults in India is quite large, showing that a significant part of the population still lacks adequate nutrition — a major development challenge.

stem: A dam built for irrigation and electricity may be seen as development by some but not by others because:
options: It benefits some people while displacing or harming others
solution: A dam may provide irrigation and power (development) for some, but it can submerge land and displace people whose livelihoods and homes are lost — so the same project can mean different things to different groups.

stem: Comparing states, the state with the highest Infant Mortality Rate among Kerala, Punjab and Bihar (per the chapter) is:
solution: Bihar, being the poorest of the three in per capita income and social facilities, has the highest infant mortality rate, while Kerala has the lowest.

stem: The chapter concludes that the measurement of development should include:
options: Income along with health, education, environment and other quality-of-life factors
solution: The chapter concludes that development cannot be measured by income alone; a combination of income and non-income factors — health, education, environment and quality of life — gives a truer picture.

stem: The reason we still use averages like per capita income, despite their limitations, is that:
options: They allow simple comparison between large groups or countries
solution: Averages are used for comparison because it is difficult to compare the incomes of every individual; a single average figure lets us compare countries or states, even though it hides internal disparities.

stem: For a country to have real development, it is important to consider whether resources being used are:
options: Sustainable, so that development continues for future generations
Being used up as fast as possible
solution: Sustainability of development is crucial: if resources are exhausted or the environment is damaged, current growth cannot be maintained, harming the prospects of future generations.

stem: Crude oil (petroleum) is used in the chapter to illustrate that:
options: Non-renewable resources have a limited stock and will get exhausted
solution: The example of the world's crude oil reserves, which will last only a few decades at current rates of use, shows that non-renewable resources are finite and their use raises the question of sustainability.

stem: The comparison of two persons or groups seeking conflicting things shows that:
options: What is development for one may not be development for another
Development is the same for all
solution: Different people may seek conflicting goals; for example, industrialists may want more dams for electricity while tribals may oppose them to protect their land — the notion of development varies among groups.

stem: National development, according to the chapter, requires considering:
options: Which programmes and policies benefit a large number of people, not just a few
Only the interests of the rich
solution: National development involves thinking about how the country as a whole can progress, giving importance to what would benefit a large number of people rather than a small group, and using fair means.

stem: Two states may have similar average income but the one with better public health and education will have:
solution: Better provision of public facilities like health and education leads to higher literacy, lower infant mortality and longer life expectancy, giving a state better human development even at the same income level.

stem: The per capita income in the Human Development Report is calculated in dollars using __________ to make comparison meaningful across countries.
solution: In the Human Development Report, per capita income is shown in dollars, calculated in a way (using purchasing power parity) that reflects what the income can actually buy, making cross-country comparison meaningful.

stem: The overall message of the chapter 'Development' is that development is:
options: A many-sided idea involving income, health, education, equity, environment and sustainability
Measured only by per capita income
solution: The chapter concludes that development is a complex, many-sided idea: it is about more than income, encompassing health, education, equality, freedom, security, a clean environment and sustainability.

stem: A country with a higher per capita income than another may still be considered less developed if it has:
options: Poorer health, education and higher inequality
solution: Higher average income does not guarantee development; a richer country with worse health outcomes, lower literacy, or greater inequality may rank lower in human development than a poorer but more equal one.

stem: The distribution of income within a country matters because:
options: A very unequal distribution can leave many people poor despite a high average income
solution: Even with a high average income, if income is very unequally distributed, a large section of people may remain poor; hence how income is shared is as important as the average itself.

stem: Which of the following best reflects the chapter's view on income versus other goals?
options: People want more income as well as non-material things like respect, freedom and security
Income and other goals are unrelated
solution: People desire a mix of goals: besides a higher income, they also want equal treatment, freedom, security and respect, and dislike discrimination — development must address all these.

stem: The chapter uses the comparison of countries and states mainly to demonstrate that:
options: Development must be judged by multiple indicators, not income alone
Income is the only thing that matters
solution: By comparing countries and Indian states on income and social indicators, the chapter demonstrates that development is best judged by a range of indicators — income, health and education together — not by income alone.

stem: In the World Development Report, per capita income is calculated in US dollars so that comparison between countries becomes possible. This income is worked out on the basis of:
options: The total population of the world
The total income of a country divided by its total population for a particular year
The income of the richest person
solution: Per capita income or average income is calculated as the total income of the country divided by its total population; in the World Development Report this is expressed in US dollars for a particular year to enable comparison between countries.
